x: 24 November 2026 · Computational Classnotes · TensorNets units of learning, 1 of 4 Two recurrent networks can translate. One reads the whole sentence into a fixed-size vector, and the other writes the translation from that vector. Sutskever, Vinyals and Le (2014) built this from deep LSTMs and reached 34.8 BLEU on English to French. This unit builds each part of their machine from plain arrays and checks it against Wolfram’s own layers. The notebook unit1_seq2seq.nb carries the same section numbers and computes every number quoted here.

t: Unit 1 · Reading a Sequence, Writing a Sequence
x: Read the reversed source into a vector, then write the target from it, one word at a time. Fig. 1 Fig. 1. The encoder–decoder. The encoder reads the reversed source and ends in the thought vector v. The decoder starts from v and writes the target, reading back each word it has just written (§2).

t: Unit 1 · Reading a Sequence, Writing a Sequence
x: A sentence and its translation rarely have the same length, and word i of one is not word i of the other. So the paper uses two networks. The encoder reads the source one word at a time and ends in a fixed-size vector v, the thought vector. The decoder starts from v and writes the target one word at a time, feeding each word back in, until it writes <EOS>: p(y1,…,yT′∣x1,…,xT)=∏t=1T′p(yt∣v,y1,…,yt−1). Three choices made it work (Section 2 of the paper): two different LSTMs for reading and writing, four layers each, and the source fed in reverse (§6).

t: Unit 1 · Reading a Sequence, Writing a Sequence
x: An LSTM keeps the hidden state h and the memory cell c. At each step it reads an input x and computes four gates from x and the previous h: i=σ(Wix+Uih+bi),f=σ(Wfx+Ufh+bf),o=σ(Wox+Uoh+bo),g=tanh(Wgx+Ugh+bg),c′=fc+ig,h′=otanh(c′). The input gate i decides how much new content g to write, the forget gate f how much old memory to keep, and the output gate o how much memory to show. The memory is updated by addition. This additive update is why information and gradients survive over long sentences. Worked by hand. Take one input and one cell, every weight 0.5 and every bias 0, start from h = c = 0 and read x = 1. Every gate sees 0.5·1 + 0.5·0 + 0 = 0.5. So i = f = o = σ(0.5) = 0.6225 and g = tanh(0.5) = 0.4621. Then c′ = 0.6225·0 + 0.6225·0.4621 = 0.2877, and h′ = 0.6225·tanh(0.2877) = 0.6225·0.2800 = 0.1743. Wolfram’s LongShortTermMemoryLayer stores exactly these twelve arrays (it calls g the memory gate). Its ports State and CellState are h and c. The forget gate decides how long memory lasts. After a single input pulse the memory is multiplied by f at every step, so it decays like fᵗ (Fig. 2). Fig. 2 Fig. 2. The memory c of a one-cell LSTM after one input pulse, for three forget-gate biases. With f = 0.95 the pulse is still 30 % present after 25 steps; with f = 0.05 it is gone after two. Checked (notebook §3): the hand computation gives h′ = 0.17427, c′ = 0.28765. Our step, copied weights and all, equals LongShortTermMemoryLayer (6 cells, 7 steps: True), also from given starting states (True). After the pulse the ratio of successive memories is σ(3) = 0.9526 exactly (True).

x: The paper stacks four LSTMs. Layer k reads the hidden states of layer k − 1. After the last source word, the final (h, c) of every layer is kept. Together they are the thought vector: 2 × 4 × 1000 = 8000 numbers in the paper’s model. Checked (notebook §4): a three-layer stack coded from arrays equals NetChain of three LSTM layers (True); its thought vector has 2 × 3 × 5 = 30 numbers, and the paper’s 8000.

t: Unit 1 · Reading a Sequence, Writing a Sequence
x: The decoder is a second deep LSTM with its own weights. Its layers start from the encoder’s final states. At each step it reads the embedding of the previous word, and a softmax turns its top hidden state into probabilities for the next word: p(next word=k)=ezk∑jezj,z=Wh+b. Worked by hand. For scores z = (2, 1, 0): e² = 7.389, e¹ = 2.718 and e⁰ = 1, with total 11.107. The probabilities are 0.665, 0.245 and 0.090. They are positive and sum to 1, and adding the same number to every score changes nothing. During training the decoder reads the correct previous word, not its own guess (teacher forcing). At test time it reads its own output, and beam search (§8) decides which outputs to keep. Checked (notebook §5): softmax(2, 1, 0) = (0.665, 0.245, 0.090), and the same after adding 10 to every score. One decoder step gives a distribution over 10 words that is positive and sums to 1, and its first layer, started from the encoder’s states, matches Wolfram’s layer (True, True, True).

t: Unit 1 · Reading a Sequence, Writing a Sequence
x: The paper feeds the source reversed: c, b, a instead of a, b, c, while the target stays α, β, γ. Nothing else changes, yet test BLEU rose from 25.9 to 30.6 (Section 3.3). The reason is distance. Put the source at positions 1…T and the target after it at T + 1…2T, with target word i aligned to source word i. Worked by hand (T = 3). Forward, a, b, c sit at 1, 2, 3 and α, β, γ at 4, 5, 6, so every pair is 3 steps apart. Reversed, a sits at 3, b at 2 and c at 1, so the gaps are 4 − 3 = 1, 5 − 2 = 3 and 6 − 1 = 5. The average is 3 both ways, but the first pair is now 1 step apart. The network can link a to α at once and build from there. Fig. 3 Fig. 3. Distance between source word i and target word i for T = 8. Forward, every pair is 8 apart. Reversed, the distances are 1, 3, 5, …, 15: the same average, but the first words are neighbours. Checked (notebook §6): T = 3 gives {3, 3, 3} and {1, 3, 5}; T = 8 gives averages 8 and 8, and shortest distances 8 and 1.

t: Unit 1 · Reading a Sequence, Writing a Sequence
x: Starting weights. Every parameter starts uniformly distributed in [−0.08, 0.08] (Section 3.4). Wolfram’s NetInitialize does this with one option, but it always sets the LSTM forget-gate biases to 1. That is a later practice, recommended by Jozefowicz, Zaremba and Sutskever (2015). To follow the paper, the notebook’s uniformInit resets those biases too. Clipping the gradient by its norm. LSTMs rarely suffer from vanishing gradients but can suffer from exploding ones. For each batch the paper computes the norm of the whole gradient, all parameters together, and rescales it if it exceeds 5: s=∥g∥2,if s>5:g←5gs. Worked by hand. g = (6, 8) has norm √(36 + 64) = 10 > 5, so it becomes (6, 8)·5/10 = (3, 4), with norm 5 and the same direction. Clamping each component to ±5 would give (5, 5) instead, which points elsewhere: its cosine with g is 70/(10·√50) = 0.990. The learning rate. The paper used plain stochastic gradient descent without momentum, with batches of 128 sentences and a rate of 0.7. After 5 epochs the rate is halved every half epoch, and training stops after 7.5 epochs (Fig. 4). Fig. 4 Fig. 4. The learning rate over the 7.5 epochs of training. Checked (notebook §7): plain NetInitialize leaves every forget-gate bias at 1.; after uniformInit every parameter of a two-layer LSTM is within ±0.08 (True). Clipping gives (3, 4), leaves (0.3, 0.4) alone, keeps the direction (cosine 1) where clamping does not (0.9899). The rate is 0.7, 0.35, 0.175 and 0.021875 at epochs 4.99, 5, 5.5 and 7.4.

t: Unit 1 · Reading a Sequence, Writing a Sequence
x: To write, the decoder must choose words. Greedy decoding takes the most likely word at each step. Beam search keeps the B most likely partial outputs instead. Each is extended by every word, and the B best extensions are kept. A hypothesis that ends in <EOS> leaves the beam and joins the finished list. The paper finds that B = 1 already works well and that B = 2 gives most of the benefit (Section 3.2). Worked by hand. A toy model writes A (0.6) or B (0.4) first. After A it hesitates: A 0.3, B 0.3, <e> 0.4. After B it almost always stops: <e> 0.95. Greedy takes A, then <e>, so its output has probability 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.24. A beam of width 2 keeps both A and B after step 1. At step 2 the six extensions are A<e> 0.24, AA 0.18, AB 0.18, B<e> 0.38, BA 0.01 and BB 0.01. The best two are both finished, and B<e> wins with 0.38. Fig. 5 Fig. 5. The search tree of the toy model. Greedy follows the dashed path; the beam of width 2 also keeps B and finds the better output (orange). Checked (notebook §8): greedy returns {<s>, A, <e>} with probability 0.24; the beam of width 2 returns {<s>, B, <e>} with 0.38.

h: 9. How big is the paper’s model?
x: An LSTM layer with nᵢₙ inputs and n cells has four gates, each with an n × nᵢₙ input matrix, an n × n state matrix and n biases: parameters=4(nnin+n2+n). Worked by hand. One layer of 1000 cells reading 1000 numbers has 4 × (1 000 000 + 1 000 000 + 1000) = 8 004 000 parameters. Eight such layers make 64 032 000. The embeddings add 160 000 × 1000 + 80 000 × 1000 = 240 000 000, and the softmax adds 80 000 × 1000 + 80 000 = 80 080 000. The total is 384 112 000, the paper’s “384M parameters”. Most of them belong to the vocabulary, not to the LSTMs. Checked (notebook §9): the formula equals Wolfram’s count for a layer with 4 inputs and 6 cells (True); the total is 384 112 000.

t: Unit 1 · Reading a Sequence, Writing a Sequence
x: Two deep LSTMs translate. One reads the whole source into the final states of its layers, and the other writes from them, one word at a time. The LSTM’s additive memory, controlled by its forget gate, carries information across the sentence. Reversing the source puts the first words next to each other. Small starting weights, norm clipping and a halving learning rate make training reliable. A narrow beam finds better outputs than greedy decoding. Next, Unit 2 turns mathematics into sequences a machine can learn from, and Unit 3 replaces the LSTM with attention.

24 November 2026 · Computational Classnotes · TensorNets units of learning, 2 of 4 A neural net can learn to integrate if integration is written as translation: the problem is one sequence and its solution is another. Lample and Charton (2019) trained a standard transformer this way, and what was new was the data. This unit builds their data machinery: trees in prefix notation, fair sampling of trees, three ways of making integration problems, and a check on every answer. Counting the trees also turns up a slip in the paper’s Equation 2. The notebook unit2_symbolic_data.nb has the same section numbers and computes every number quoted here.

Trees. u is a unary node, b a binary node and • a leaf. A tree is stored as its list of arities in prefix order, for example {2, 0, 1, 0} for b • u •. Counts. D(e, n) is the number of ways to complete a tree with e empty slots and n internal nodes still to place. Cₙ is the Catalan number and Sₙ the large Schröder number. L, p₁ and p₂ are the numbers of leaf values, unary operators and binary operators. Variable. In the notebook the variable is Wolfram’s formal symbol \[FormalX], shown as a dotted x. Numbering. Sections 2–9 here match notebook Sections 2–9; notebook Section 1 is the toolkit. Every number below was returned by the Wolfram kernel (Wolfram 15.0). Paper. G. Lample, F. Charton, Deep Learning for Symbolic Mathematics, ICLR 2020, arXiv:1912.01412. “Section n” and “Appendix X” refer to the paper; “§n” refers to this unit.

An expression is a tree, and its prefix sequence is the tree read node first. Fig. 1 Fig. 1. The tree of 2 + 3 × (5 + 2). Read node first, then the children from left to right, it gives the prefix sequence add 2 mul 3 add 5 2 (§3).

Write a problem as a sequence of symbols and its solution as another. A sequence-to-sequence model (Units 1 and 3) can then learn to map one to the other. For integration the problem is f, and the solution is a function F with F′ = f. Three things are needed: a way to write expressions as sequences (§3), a supply of correct problem–solution pairs (§4–§6), and a way to check what the model writes (§7).

Prefix (Polish) notation writes each node before its children. Every symbol has a fixed arity: add, sub, mul, div and pow take two arguments; exp, log, sin and cos take one; numbers and x take none. So prefix needs no parentheses, and trees and prefix sequences correspond one to one (Section 2.1). Worked by hand. Keep a counter of subtrees still owed, starting at 1. Each symbol fills one slot and opens as many as its arity, so the counter changes by arity − 1. For add 2 mul 3 add 5 2 it runs 1 → 2 → 1 → 2 → 1 → 2 → 1 → 0. It reaches 0 exactly at the last token, so the sequence is one complete tree. It has 7 tokens, against 9 for the infix form 2 + 3 × ( 5 + 2 ). A sequence is a valid tree exactly when the counter stays positive until the last token and ends at 0. An integer is a sign token followed by its digits: −305 is INT- 3 0 5. Ten digits and two signs cover every integer. Checked (notebook §3): the counter is {1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 0}. add x INT+ 3 is valid; add x, add x x x and INT+ alone are not. −305 ↔︎ INT- 3 0 5 and 12 → INT+ 1 2. Prefix and back returns the same expression for three examples and for all 276 well-formed random expressions of 300 drawn.

To sample fairly one must first count. The first empty slot of a tree is a leaf, a unary node or a binary node (Appendix C): D(0,n)=0(n>0),D(e,0)=1,D(e,n)=D(e−1,n)+D(e,n−1)+D(e+1,n−1). D(1, n) counts whole trees with n internal nodes. With binary nodes only, the middle term is dropped and D(1, n) = Cₙ. With unary and binary nodes it is the large Schröder number Sₙ, which satisfies the paper’s Equation 1, (n + 1)Sₙ = 3(2n − 1)Sₙ₋₁ − (n − 2)Sₙ₋₂. Worked by hand. The trees with two internal nodes are u u •, u b • •, b u • •, b • u •, b b • • • and b • b • •, so S₂ = 6. By the recurrence, D(1, 2) = D(0, 2) + D(1, 1) + D(2, 1) = 0 + 2 + 4 = 6. Here D(1, 1) = 2 (u • and b • •), and D(2, 1) = D(1, 1) + D(2, 0) + D(3, 0) = 2 + 1 + 1 = 4. Counting expressions, and a correction. An expression is a tree whose leaves take one of L values, unary nodes one of p₁ operators and binary nodes one of p₂. So each tree counts L^leaves p₁^unary p₂^binary times, and the total Eₙ satisfies E(z) = L + p₁zE(z) + p₂zE(z)². The paper’s Equation 2, as printed, ends in −p₁(n − 2)Eₙ₋₂. Expanding the square root gives (1−p1z)2−4Lp2z=1−2(p1+2Lp2)z+p12z2, so the last coefficient is p₁², not p₁. Appendix B writes p₁z² for the last term, and the p₁ carries into Equation 2. The corrected recurrence is (n+1)En=(p1+2Lp2)(2n−1)En−1−p12(n−2)En−2,E0=L,E1=p1L+p2L2. The two forms agree when p₁ is 0 or 1, the cases the paper checks against Equation 1 and the Catalan numbers. Fig. 2 Fig. 2. The number of binary trees, unary–binary trees and expressions with n internal nodes, on a log scale. With the paper’s 11 leaves, 15 unary and 4 binary operators there are about 5.4 × 10³³ expressions with 15 internal nodes. Checked (notebook §4): the six trees, with D(1, 2) = 6, D(1, 1) = 2 and D(2, 1) = 4. D(1, n) equals Cₙ (binary) and Sₙ (unary–binary) for n ≤ 12, and the number of trees listed one by one for n ≤ 7. For L = 4, p₁ = 3, p₂ = 2 the corrected Equation 2 equals the count of every tree for n ≤ 6. The printed form agrees at n = 2 and first differs at n = 3 (19 822 against the true 19 756). With p₁ = 1 the printed form is right for n ≤ 10. For the paper’s settings, E₁₅ = 5.43 × 10³³.

A naive recursive generator picks binary or unary with fixed probabilities, then splits the remaining nodes at random. It favours some shapes. The paper samples every tree with n internal nodes equally often. Start with one empty slot, e = 1, and choose the position k and arity a of the next internal node with P(k,unary)=D(e−k,n−1)D(e,n),P(k,binary)=D(e−k+1,n−1)D(e,n),k=0,…,e−1. The k slots before it become leaves. Then e becomes e − k (unary) or e − k + 1 (binary), and n falls by 1 (Appendix C, Algorithm 2). With binary nodes only, the same idea is Algorithm 1. Worked by hand (n = 2). With e = 1 only k = 0 is possible. P(0, unary) = D(1, 1)/D(1, 2) = 2/6 = 1/3, and P(0, binary) = D(2, 1)/D(1, 2) = 4/6 = 2/3. Of the six trees in §4, two start with u and four with b. A fair first choice is exactly the fraction of trees that start that way. Fig. 3 Fig. 3. Counts of the 22 trees with three internal nodes in 22 000 samples. The paper’s algorithm gives each about 1000. The naive generator gives the most common shape 3637 times and the rarest 314. Checked (notebook §5): the first-step weights are 2 and 4 out of 6. Algorithm 2 produces all 22 trees and is consistent with uniform (χ² p-value above 0.001); the naive generator is not (p below 10⁻⁶). Algorithm 1 is uniform over the 14 binary trees with four internal nodes.

Forward (FWD). Draw f and ask a computer algebra system for its integral. This is slow, and it only contains integrals that system can find. Backward (BWD). Draw F and differentiate it. The pair (F′, F) is always available, and it is fast. Integration by parts (IBP). If the integral of F′G is already known, the integral of FG′ follows with no computer algebra system (Section 3): ∫FG′dx=FG−∫F′Gdx. Worked by hand. Take F = x and G = sin x, so FG′ = x cos x. The known integral needed is ∫ sin x dx = −cos x. So ∫ x cos x dx = x sin x + cos x. Differentiating gives sin x + x cos x − sin x = x cos x. Differentiation lengthens expressions. So in BWD data the problem is usually longer than its solution, and in FWD data the reverse. The paper notes that a model trained only on BWD data learns that integration shortens expressions, which FWD data contradicts (Section 3, Table 1). Method Pairs Mean problem length Mean solution length FWD 30 7.07 12.7 BWD 60 8.33 7.13 Checked (notebook §6): every FWD and BWD pair is correct, by differentiation, and BWD problems are longer than their solutions on average (True, True, True). Three rounds of IBP over the BWD pairs of x, x², x³, sin x, cos x and eˣ found 9 new pairs, all correct, without calling Integrate. Among them is ±x³ sin x, whose integral, −x³ cos x + 3x² sin x + 6x cos x − 6 sin x, is the paper’s example of a solution that random generation would almost never produce.

h: 7. Checking answers instead of trusting them
x: Nothing stops a decoder from writing an invalid prefix sequence, and such hypotheses are thrown away. An integral can be checked by differentiating it. So the paper checks every hypothesis in the beam, not only the most likely one. “Beam size 10” means that at least one of the ten hypotheses was correct (Section 4.4). A constant of integration does not matter. Checked (notebook §7): for ∫ x cos x dx, the hypotheses x sin x + cos x and x sin x + cos x + 3 are accepted; x sin x and the unfinished sequence add mul x sin are rejected ({True, True, False, False}).

Write (x + 1)² in prefix notation and run the counter of §3 over it. Compute D(1, 3) from the recurrence, using D(1, 2) = 6. With L = 2, p₁ = 2 and p₂ = 1, compute E₃ from the corrected and from the printed Equation 2. Which equals the count? For n = 3, what is the probability that Algorithm 2 makes the root binary? Use integration by parts, as in §6, to find ∫ x eˣ dx, and check it by differentiating. Answers (notebook §8): (1) pow add INT+ 1 x INT+ 2; the counter runs 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 0, the digits counting as part of their integer. (2) D(1, 3) = D(1, 2) + D(2, 2) = 6 + 16 = 22. (3) The corrected form gives 352, which equals the count; the printed form gives 356. (4) D(2, 2)/D(1, 3) = 16/22 = 8/11. (5) x eˣ − eˣ, whose derivative is x eˣ.

Mathematics becomes data in three steps. Expressions are written as trees in prefix notation, which is short, needs no parentheses and can be read back with a single counter. Trees are sampled uniformly by counting how many ways each choice can be completed. Correct pairs come from differentiating (BWD) and from integration by parts (IBP), with no computer algebra system. Because an answer can be checked, the model need not be trusted: every hypothesis in the beam is verified. Next, Unit 3 builds the transformer that learns from such data, and Unit 4 uses all of this on ⨂/⨁ expressions.

24 November 2026 · Computational Classnotes · TensorNets units of learning, 3 of 4 The transformer drops recurrence: every word looks at every other word at once, through attention, and word order is added as a code. Vaswani et al. (2017) built a translator from attention alone and trained it faster and better than recurrent models. This unit builds each part twice, once from plain arrays to see the mathematics and once as a Wolfram net from primitive layers to train it, and checks that the two agree. The notebook unit3_transformer.nb has the same section numbers and computes every number quoted here.

Shapes. A sequence is a matrix with one row per position. dmodel is the width of each row, h the number of heads, dₖ = dmodel/h, and dff the width of the feed-forward layer. The base model has dmodel = 512, h = 8, dff = 2048 and 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers. Two versions. Every part is coded from arrays (sdpa, mha, pe, ffn, layerNorm, encoderLayer, decoderLayer) and as a net (mhaNet, peNet, ffnNet, encoderLayerNet, decoderLayerNet). The array versions read their weights out of the nets, so the comparison is exact. Numbering. Sections 2–16 here match notebook Sections 2–16; notebook Section 1 is the toolkit. Every number below was returned by the Wolfram kernel (Wolfram 15.0). Paper. A. Vaswani, N. Shazeer, N. Parmar, J. Uszkoreit, L. Jones, A. N. Gomez, Ł. Kaiser, I. Polosukhin, Attention Is All You Need, NeurIPS 2017, arXiv:1706.03762. “Section n” refers to the paper; “§n” refers to this unit.

An encoder–decoder in which every layer is attention plus a small feed-forward network. Fig. 1 Fig. 1. The transformer. Each encoder layer is self-attention, then a feed-forward network, each wrapped as add & LayerNorm. Each decoder layer adds masked self-attention and attention over the encoder’s output (orange arrow). The paper uses N = 6.

An LSTM (Unit 1) reads one word after another. The first word reaches the last only through every step between them, and the steps cannot run in parallel. The transformer lets every position look at every other position directly. Each position asks a question (its query), every position offers a key and a value, and the output is an average of the values weighted by how well the keys match the query.

Stack the queries as rows of Q, the keys as rows of K and the values as rows of V. Compare every query with every key by a dot product, divide by √dₖ (§4), take the softmax of each row and average the values with those weights (Section 3.2.1): Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QK𝖳dk)V. Worked by hand. Let q = (1, 0), with keys k₁ = (1, 0) and k₂ = (0, 1), values v₁ = (1, 0) and v₂ = (0, 1), and dₖ = 2. The scores are q·k₁/√2 = 0.7071 and q·k₂/√2 = 0. The weights are e0.7071/(e0.7071 + 1) = 2.028/3.028 = 0.670 and 1/3.028 = 0.330. The output is 0.670 v₁ + 0.330 v₂ = (0.670, 0.330): mostly the value of the matching key. Checked (notebook §3): {{0.670, 0.330}}. The formula from arrays equals Wolfram’s AttentionLayer["Dot", "ScoreRescaling" -> "DimensionSqrt"] for 4 queries and 7 keys, and every row of weights sums to 1 (True, True).

If the components of q and k are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then q·k = q₁k₁ + … + q_d k_d is a sum of dₖ independent terms, each of variance 1. So Var(q·k) = dₖ and Var(q·k/√dₖ) = 1 (footnote 4 of the paper). For dₖ = 64 the unscaled scores are about ±8, the softmax is nearly one-hot, and its gradient is tiny. Fig. 2 Fig. 2. The mean largest softmax weight over 10 random keys. Without scaling it climbs towards 1 as dₖ grows; with scaling it stays near 0.3 for every dₖ. Checked (notebook §4): for dₖ = 64 the measured variances are 63.6 unscaled and 0.994 scaled. The largest weight is above 0.75 unscaled and below 0.6 scaled (True, True).

A mask is added to the scores before the softmax: 0 where attention is allowed, and a very large negative number where it is not, so those weights become 0. A padding mask hides padding at the end of short sequences. A causal mask stops position i of the decoder from seeing positions after i, so it cannot read the word it must predict (Section 3.2.3). Worked by hand. For three positions the causal mask is ((0, −∞, −∞), (0, 0, −∞), (0, 0, 0)). Row 1 sees only position 1, so its weights are (1, 0, 0) whatever the scores. Row 2 shares its weight between positions 1 and 2, and row 3 sees all three. Fig. 3 Fig. 3. Attention weights with a causal mask, for 6 positions. Everything above the diagonal is exactly 0. Checked (notebook §5): changing positions 5 and 6 leaves outputs 1–4 unchanged; the array mask equals AttentionLayer with "Mask" -> "Causal"; with 4 real keys, changing the 2 padding keys changes nothing (True, True, True). In Wolfram, padding needs no mask: sequences of different lengths are "Varying" dimensions, and NetTrain pads and masks them itself.

One attention with dmodel-dimensional queries is replaced by h attentions of dₖ = dmodel/h dimensions each, on different learned projections. Their outputs are joined and projected once more (Section 3.2.2): MultiHead(Q,K,V)=Concat(head1,…,headh)WO,headi=Attention(QWiQ,KWiK,VWiV). As a Wolfram net, mhaNet uses LinearLayer for the projections (all heads at once), ReshapeLayer to split the dmodel features into h groups of dₖ, AttentionLayer with "MultiHead" -> True for the h attentions, FlattenLayer to join them and a last LinearLayer for W^O. Worked by hand. In the base model dmodel = 512 and h = 8, so each head works in dₖ = 64 dimensions. The four projections are 512 × 512 matrices with 512 biases each: 4 × (512² + 512) = 1 050 624 parameters, whatever the number of heads. Checked (notebook §6): the net from primitive layers equals multi-head attention from arrays (d = 16, h = 4), also with the causal mask. It has 4(d² + d) parameters, the same for 1 head as for 4, and 1 050 624 for the base model (True, True, True, 1050624).

Attention by itself ignores word order, so a position code is added to each embedding (Section 3.5). Each pair of components is a sine and a cosine of the position, with wavelengths from 2π to 10000 · 2π: PE(pos,2i)=sin(pos/100002i/dmodel),PE(pos,2i+1)=cos(pos/100002i/dmodel). Worked by hand. Take dmodel = 4 and pos = 1. For i = 0 the frequency is 1, giving (sin 1, cos 1) = (0.8415, 0.5403). For i = 1 it is 1/10000^(2/4) = 0.01, giving (sin 0.01, cos 0.01) = (0.0100, 0.99995). Fast components tell nearby positions apart; slow ones tell distant ones apart. Fig. 4 Fig. 4. The position code of positions 0–99 (across) in 64 dimensions (down). The first dimensions oscillate fast; the last ones hardly change. The paper chose sinusoids because, for every offset k, one fixed matrix Mₖ (a rotation in each pair of components) gives PE(pos + k) = Mₖ PE(pos) for every position. “k places later” is therefore a linear operation. In Wolfram, writing cos x = sin(x + π/2) makes every component sin(pos ω + φ): a frozen LinearLayer from the position, then Sin. That is peNet. Checked (notebook §7): PE(1) = (0.8415, 0.5403, 0.0100, 0.99995). One rotation per offset works for k = 1, 5 and 17. PE(pos)·PE(pos + 7) is the same for every pos. peNet (SequenceIndicesLayer, a frozen LinearLayer, Sin) adds exactly these codes for any length (True, True, True).

After attention, every position goes through the same two-layer network on its own: dmodel → dff → dmodel with a ReLU between (Section 3.3). Every sub-layer is wrapped in a residual connection and followed by layer normalisation (Section 3.1): FFN(x)=max(0,xW1+b1)W2+b2,output=LayerNorm(x+Sublayer(x)),LayerNorm(v)=γv−v‾varv+ε+β. The residual lets the signal and its gradient pass straight through. The normalisation keeps every position’s vector at mean 0 and variance 1, before a learned scale γ and shift β. Worked by hand. LayerNorm of v = (1, 2, 3) with γ = 1, β = 0: the mean is 2 and the variance (1 + 0 + 1)/3 = 2/3. With ε = 0.001, √(2/3 + 0.001) = 0.8171, so the result is (−1.2238, 0, 1.2238). Without ε it would be ±1.2247. Checked (notebook §8): Wolfram’s NormalizationLayer[2, 2] gives (−1.2238, 0, 1.2238), with ε = 0.001. ffnNet equals the formula at every position, and NormalizationLayer equals LayerNorm from arrays with a random γ and β (True, True). The paper normalises after the residual sum (post-norm). Many later transformers normalise before the sub-layer (pre-norm), which is easier to train when there are many layers.

h: 9. One encoder layer and one decoder layer
x: An encoder layer is self-attention, then the feed-forward network, each wrapped as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)). A decoder layer has three sub-layers: causal self-attention over the output so far; attention over the encoder’s output, with queries from the decoder and keys and values from the encoder; and the feed-forward network (Fig. 1). Checked (notebook §9): both layer nets equal their array versions, and the decoder is causal: output i does not change when a later output position changes (True, True, True).

The paper uses one weight matrix for the input embedding, the output embedding and the projection before the softmax, and multiplies the embeddings by √dmodel (Section 3.4). In Wolfram the sharing is NetSharedArray. EmbeddingLayer stores a V × d matrix, and LinearLayer[V] on d-dimensional inputs stores a V × d matrix too, so one array serves both. Checked (notebook §10): the embedding and the output projection are one array, stored once: 20 × 8 = 160 shared weights plus 20 output biases, 180 in all (True, 180).

The training target is not one-hot. With ε = 0.1 and K classes it puts 1 − ε + ε/K on the right class and ε/K on each of the others: q=(1−ε)onehot(y)+ε/K,loss=−∑kqklogpk. The model learns to be less sure. The paper reports that this hurts perplexity but improves accuracy and BLEU (Section 5.4). Worked by hand. K = 4, right class 3, ε = 0.1: q = (0.025, 0.025, 0.925, 0.025). If the model predicts q itself, the loss is −(0.925 ln 0.925 + 3 × 0.025 ln 0.025) = 0.0721 + 0.2767 = 0.349. If it is 99.9 % sure of class 3, the three small classes alone cost 0.075 × ln 3000 = 0.601. Being too sure is now penalised. Fig. 5 Fig. 5. The label-smoothed loss for K = 4, as a function of the probability given to the right class. Its minimum is at 0.925 (dashed), not at 1. Checked (notebook §11): q = (0.025, 0.025, 0.925, 0.025); losses 0.349 and 0.601.

Adam with β₁ = 0.9, β₂ = 0.98 and ε = 10⁻⁹. The learning rate rises linearly for the first 4000 steps, then falls as 1/√step (Section 5.3): lrate=dmodel−0.5⋅min(step−0.5,step⋅warmup−1.5),warmup=4000. The warm-up protects the young network from large, badly aimed steps. Worked by hand. The two terms are equal when step^−0.5 = step · 4000^−1.5, that is at step 4000. There the rate is 512^−0.5 × 4000^−0.5 = 0.04419 × 0.01581 = 6.99 × 10⁻⁴, the peak. Fig. 6 Fig. 6. The learning rate over the first 40 000 steps. Checked (notebook §12): the peak is 0.000699, at step 4000 (True). In Wolfram the schedule is a factor of the learning rate: NetTrain[…, Method -> {"ADAM", "Beta1" -> 0.9, "Beta2" -> 0.98, "LearningRate" -> peak, "LearningRateSchedule" -> (warmRate[#]/peak &)}]. Unit 4 does this.

h: 13. Beam search with a length penalty
x: Unit 1’s beam search keeps the B best partial outputs. Its scores are sums of log-probabilities, which only fall as a hypothesis grows, so plain beam search prefers short outputs. The paper uses beam size 4 and divides each finished hypothesis’s log-probability by a length penalty with α = 0.6 (Section 6.1, from Wu et al. 2016): score(Y)=logP(Y∣X)lp(Y),lp(Y)=(5+|Y|6)α. Worked by hand. Take a short hypothesis with log P = −2.0 and 2 tokens, and a long one with −2.6 and 8 tokens. Without the penalty the short one wins. With α = 0.6, lp(2) = (7/6)^0.6 = 1.097 and lp(8) = (13/6)^0.6 = 1.590. The scores become −1.823 and −1.635, and the long one wins. Checked (notebook §13): {1.097, 1.590, −1.823, −1.635}.

h: 14. How big is the base model?
x: Worked by hand. One attention block has 4(512² + 512) = 1 050 624 parameters. The feed-forward network has 512 × 2048 + 2048 + 2048 × 512 + 512 = 2 099 712, and one LayerNorm has 2 × 512 = 1024. So an encoder layer has 3 152 384 parameters and a decoder layer 4 204 032. Six of each make 44 138 496. The shared embedding adds 37 000 × 512 = 18 944 000, and the softmax biases 37 000. The total is 63 119 496, within 3 % of the 65M in the paper’s Table 3. The exact figure depends on the vocabulary and on what is counted. Checked (notebook §14): the per-layer counts {1 050 624, 2 099 712, 1024}, the total 63 119 496, and the per-layer formulas agree with Wolfram’s counts for the small layers of §9 (True).

Repeat §3 with q = (2, 0). Does the output move towards v₁ or away from it? With dₖ = 16 and no scaling, what is the standard deviation of q·k? Compute PE(2) for dmodel = 4. With K = 10 and ε = 0.1, what probability does the smoothed target give the right class? After the peak, at which step is the learning rate of §12 half its peak? Answers (notebook §15): (1) (0.804, 0.196): a better match gives v₁ more weight. (2) 4. (3) (sin 2, cos 2, sin 0.02, cos 0.02) = (0.909, −0.416, 0.020, 0.9998). (4) 0.91. (5) Step 16 000, since the rate falls as 1/√step.

Attention is a weighted average, softmax(QKᵀ/√dₖ)V, where the √dₖ keeps the softmax from saturating. Masks decide who may look at whom. Several heads attend in different subspaces for the price of one. Sinusoidal codes add order in a way that makes shifts linear. Each sub-layer is wrapped as LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)), and encoder and decoder layers are built from these parts alone. Shared embeddings, label smoothing, warm-up and a length penalty complete the recipe. Every part built from primitive Wolfram layers equals its array version. Next, Unit 4 assembles these nets into a transformer that expands ⨂/⨁ expressions, and trains it.

24 November 2026 · Computational Classnotes · TensorNets units of learning, 4 of 4 This unit puts Units 1–3 to work on our own problem: given an expression such as (a⨁b)⨂c, write its expansion a⨂c ⨁ b⨂c. The data come from Unit 2, the net from Unit 3 and the decoding from Units 1 and 3. A net with 59 950 numbers, trained for under four minutes on a laptop CPU, writes the exact expansion for 87 of 100 unseen expressions. With a beam of four and an exact checker, 97 of the 100 are solved. The notebook unit4_build_your_own.nb has the same section numbers and computes every number quoted here.

Expressions. Atoms a, b, c, d; ⨂ is the tensor product and ⨁ the direct sum. ⨂ binds tighter than ⨁ and distributes over it on both sides. ⨂ is not commutative. Words. A word is an ordered ⨂-product of atoms. An expanded expression is a ⨁ of words. Tokens. The net reads infix tokens and writes prefix tokens (Unit 2) from one vocabulary of 10: <s>, </s>, a, b, c, d, ⨂, ⨁, (, ). Numbering. Sections 2–11 here match notebook Sections 2–11; notebook Section 1 is the toolkit. Every number below was returned by the Wolfram kernel (Wolfram 15.0, CPU). Trained net. unit4_build_your_own_nets.nb holds it as ownNet = Uncompress["…"].

Expansion can multiply the length of an expression, which makes the task harder than copying. Fig. 1 Fig. 1. Source and target lengths in tokens for 3000 random pairs. Each point is a length pair that occurs. Above the dashed line the expansion is longer than the expression (28.8 % of pairs).

⨂ distributes over ⨁ on both sides: (A⊕B)⊗C=A⊗C⊕B⊗C,A⊗(B⊕C)=A⊗B⊕A⊗C. Expanding writes an expression as a ⨁ of words. The source is the expression as one would type it, and the target is the expansion in prefix notation. Each ⨂ of two sums multiplies the number of words, so the target can be much longer than the source (Fig. 1). Checked (notebook §2): 28.8 % of 3000 random pairs have a target longer than the source.

Trees are drawn uniformly with Algorithm 1 of Unit 2: 1 to 5 operators, each ⨂ or ⨁, over the atoms a, b, c and d. Because ⨂ binds tighter than ⨁, the source needs parentheses only around a ⨁ that sits under a ⨂. Pairs with a source over 25 tokens or a target over 40 are dropped. Worked by hand. The tree ⨂(⨁(a, b), c) is ⨂ ⨁ a b c in prefix. In infix its left child is a ⨁ under a ⨂, so it is bracketed: ( a ⨁ b ) ⨂ c, 7 tokens. The tree ⨁(a, ⨂(b, c)) needs no brackets: a ⨁ b ⨂ c, 5 tokens. Checked (notebook §3): the two infix forms are as above. The sampler reaches all 14 binary trees with four operators, each between 944 and 1046 times in 14 000 samples.

An expression is a list of words. ⨁ joins two lists; ⨂ multiplies every word on the left by every word on the right, keeping their order: words(x)={x},words(A⊕B)=words(A)∪words(B),words(A⊗B)={uv:u∈words(A),v∈words(B)}. Two expressions are equal when their lists of words agree up to order. This is the check tnEquivalentQ makes in TensorNets, here called equivalentQ. Worked by hand. For (a⨁b)⨂(c⨁d), words(a⨁b) = {a, b} and words(c⨁d) = {c, d}. Their product is {ac, ad, bc, bd}: four words of two atoms each. In prefix, as a right-nested sum of right-nested products, it is ⨁ ⨂ a c ⨁ ⨂ a d ⨁ ⨂ b c ⨂ b d: 15 tokens from a source of 11. Checked (notebook §4): the words and the 15 tokens above. a⨂c ⨁ b⨂c is accepted in either order, and c⨂a ⨁ c⨂b is rejected because the order of factors matters. For 500 random pairs the target is equivalent to the source (True, False, True).

This is the encoder–decoder of Unit 3, made small: d = 32, 4 heads, dff = 128, and 2 encoder and 2 decoder layers. Source and target share one vocabulary, so one array (NetSharedArray["W"]) serves the encoder embedding, the decoder embedding and the output projection. The decoder reads the target without its last token and predicts it without its first (teacher forcing). A frozen EmbeddingLayer, whose rows are the smoothed targets, turns each target index into the label-smoothed distribution (ε = 0.1). The loss is the cross-entropy against it. Worked by hand. By the formulas of Unit 3, with d = 32 and dff = 128: attention 4(32² + 32) = 4224; feed-forward 32·128 + 128 + 128·32 + 32 = 8352; LayerNorm 64. So an encoder layer has 12 704 numbers and a decoder layer 16 992, and two of each make 59 392. The shared embedding adds 320 and the output biases 10. The frozen arrays add 100 (smoothing) and 128 (the two position layers). The total is 59 950. Checked (notebook §5): 59 950 arrays, and one shared array for the three embeddings (True).

There are 12 000 training pairs and 100 test pairs, and no test source appears in the training set. Training uses Adam with β₂ = 0.98, the warm-up schedule of Unit 3 with 400 warm-up steps, batches of 64 and 40 rounds. Fig. 2 Fig. 2. The training loss per round. It cannot reach 0: with label smoothing its floor is the entropy of the smoothed target (dashed). Worked by hand. With 10 tokens and ε = 0.1, the smoothed target gives 0.91 to the right token and 0.01 to each of the others. Its entropy is −(0.91 ln 0.91 + 9 × 0.01 ln 0.01) = 0.0858 + 0.4145 = 0.500. A perfect model would score 0.500, not 0. Checked (notebook §6): 12 000 and 100 pairs, trained in 208 s. The floor is 0.5003. The loss fell from 1.509 to 0.508, by more than half, and stays above the floor (True, True).

Each test source is decoded three ways: greedy, a beam of width 1; a beam of width 4 with the length penalty α = 0.6; the same beam, constrained by the prefix grammar. The grammar uses Unit 2’s counter: </s> is allowed only when the tree is complete, and nothing else is allowed then. Every answer is checked by the oracle. As in Lample and Charton, “any in beam” counts a source as solved if any hypothesis in the beam passes the check. Worked by hand. After ⨁ a the counter is 1 + (2 − 1) + (0 − 1) = 1. One subtree is still owed, so </s> is forbidden and an atom or an operator must follow. After ⨁ a b the counter is 0: the tree is complete, and only </s> is allowed. The beam adds alternatives, and the checker picks out a correct one for 97 of the 100 sources. Here every verified top answer also has the oracle’s exact token order. Updated 23 November 2026, 04:05 UTC · Neural nets that parse, evaluate and simplify tensor-algebra expressions in ⨂ (tensor product) and ⨁ (direct sum). Wolfram Language first; Python follows later. By Dara O Shayda and Hikari Noor Hoshino (星野ヌール) AI System Programming Group

The work is split into three separate nets, since the three tasks differ in kind: parsing is sequence-to-sequence translation;1 simplification is a sequence of decisions; evaluation is regression. Each net is paired with an exact symbolic counterpart, which labels its training data and checks its answers. Neural nets have been shown to learn symbolic mathematics from generated data2; here they are never trusted alone. The nets decide; the exact engine executes. As a result, every rewrite the system performs is mathematically sound, whatever the quality of the nets. Terms marked † are explained in detail, with examples, in Appendix A. Task Net Kind Exact counterpart (oracle) Parse tnParserNet transformer encoder–decoder†3, tokens → prefix tree tnRefParse (recursive descent, as in tensor_parser.py4) Simplify tnPolicyNet transformer encoder, two heads: which rule, at which node†; a policy net5 tnOracleStep (first applicable rule, preorder scan†) Evaluate tnValueNet transformer encoder, pooled regression†; a value net6 tnDimension, tnTermCount, tnNumeric

Lexer (tnLex, deterministic)†: identifiers become atom slots x1 … x8 in order of first appearance, so the nets learn structure rather than names. Operator spellings (⨁ ⊕ (+) +, ⨂ ⊗ (x) *, ^ ^⊗ ^⨂) are kept as distinct tokens; recognising them is part of the parser’s task. 0/𝟎 is the zero space, 1/𝟙 the unit space†. Tree: binary heads tnS[a,b] (⨁), tnP[a,b] (⨂), tnE[n,a] (tensor power), atoms tnX[i], tnZero, tnUnit. Binary heads make the prefix form unambiguous; associativity is a rewrite rule. Prefix (Polish) form†7 — (a⨁b)⨂c → P S x1 x2 x3. It is the parser’s output and the input of the other two nets. Its token k is node k of the tree in preorder, which is how the policy net points at a node.

Architecture†: token + position embeddings; encoder of L self-attention blocks; decoder of L blocks (causal self-attention, cross-attention to the encoder, feed-forward), each with residual connection and layer normalisation; softmax over the output vocabulary. Defaults d = 128, 4 heads, L = 3. Training†: teacher forcing on random trees written in random spellings (random glyphs, spacing and redundant parentheses), target = the tree’s prefix form. Decoding: greedy and grammar-constrained. This is a simple form of grammar-constrained generation8. A counter of subtrees still owed forbids premature ends, and forbids atom slots beyond those in the input, so the output is always a well-formed tree. Use: tnParse runs the net and checks it against the reference parser. With Method -> Automatic, the reference result is returned whenever the two differ, and the disagreement is reported. With Method -> "Net", the net’s own answer is returned.

Rules (all exact and sound; term rewriting in the usual sense9): ZeroSum, ZeroProd, UnitProd, PowerExpand, DistRight, DistLeft, AssocSum, AssocProd, FactorLeft, FactorRight, PowerFold. Goals: "Expand": distribute ⨂ over ⨁, remove 0 and 𝟙, expand powers, right-associate; "Factor": the reverse — take common factors out and fold powers; "Simplify": Expand, then Factor, keeping the result only if it is no longer than the input. Architecture†: the goal token is prepended to the prefix sequence; encoder as above; the rule head reads the goal position, the node head scores every position. Inference: the exact engine lists every legal (rule, node) pair, and the net’s probabilities choose among them. An illegal step can therefore never be taken, and Expand always terminates in its normal form. Verification: every result is checked by tnEquivalentQ. Both sides are expanded into words (ordered ⨂-factors) and compared as multisets. ⨁ is commutative up to natural isomorphism; ⨂ order is never changed.

Input: prefix tokens, plus each atom’s log₂ dimension. Output: log₂(1 + dimension), log₂(1 + number of terms after expansion), and log₂(1 + Expand steps) — a pooled regression†. Purpose: a fast cost estimate. For instance, it can warn before an expansion that would grow exponentially (the caveat in CONTEXT.md10), and later it can guide a search for shorter factorisations. Exact values always come from the symbolic evaluator and are reported beside the estimate. Numeric evaluation (⨂ → Kronecker product11; ⨁ → block-diagonal or concatenation) is left to tnNumeric: a net would add nothing but error there.

h: Appendix A — Terms explained, with examples
x: The running example throughout is the expression (a⨁b)⨂c.

h: A.1 Lexer (tnLex, deterministic) and atom slots
x: Definition. A lexer cuts a string into tokens, the smallest meaningful pieces: names, operators, parentheses and numbers. tnLex is deterministic: it is ordinary code, not a net, and the same string always gives the same tokens. Whenever it meets a name (an identifier), it replaces the name with an atom slot: x1 for the first distinct name, x2 for the second, and so on up to x8. The real names are kept in a separate list, so the result can be printed with them afterwards. Why. The meaning of (a⨁b)⨂c does not depend on the letters chosen. (V⨁W)⨂U and (ψ'⨁φ_2)⨂H have exactly the same structure. With slots, the nets see one pattern instead of thousands of spellings of it, and so learn structure rather than names. Examples. Input string Tokens Atoms (a⨁b)⨂c ( x1 ⨁ x2 ) ⨂ x3 {a, b, c} (V⨁W)⨂U ( x1 ⨁ x2 ) ⨂ x3 {V, W, U} a⨂b⨁a x1 ⨂ x2 ⨁ x1 {a, b} (a repeated name keeps its slot) (V ⊕ W)^2 ( x1 ⊕ x2 ) ^ n2 {V, W} Operator spellings are kept as they were typed (⨁ and ⊕ remain different tokens), because learning that they mean the same thing is part of the parser’s task. (x) is always read as a ⨂ spelling, never as a name, so the letters x and X are not used as names.

h: A.2 0/𝟎 is the zero space, 1/𝟙 the unit space
x: Definition. The zero space15 is the vector space with one element, the zero vector. Its dimension is 0. For every space V: V ⨁ 0 ≅ V, and V ⨂ 0 ≅ 0. The unit space is the ground field itself (for example ℝ or ℂ), a space of dimension 1. For every space V: V ⨂ 𝟙 ≅ V. It plays the part that the number 1 plays in multiplication. Spelling. Either may be typed as a plain digit (0, 1) or as the double-struck character (𝟎, 𝟙). A digit directly after ^ is an exponent, not a space: a^2 is a⨂a. Any other number is an error. Examples (with tnSimplify[…, "Simplify"]): Input Result Rule that removed it a ⨁ 0 a ZeroSum (a⨁b) ⨂ 0 0 ZeroProd a ⨂ 𝟙 ⨂ b a ⨂ b UnitProd (V⊕W)⨂(V⊕W) ⨂ 𝟙 ⨁ 0 (V ⨁ W)^2 ZeroSum, UnitProd; expansion; then FactorLeft, FactorRight, PowerFold In numeric evaluation, 𝟙 is the 1 × 1 matrix {{1}}.

Definition. In prefix form, each operator is written before its operands, so no parentheses are needed: - S stands for ⨁ (two operands); - P stands for ⨂ (two operands); - E2 … E9 stand for the tensor powers ^2 … ^9 (one operand). Reading the tree in preorder16 means visiting a node first, then its left subtree, then its right subtree. Read this way, the nodes come out in exactly the order of the prefix tokens. Example. (a⨁b)⨂c is the tree P(S(x1, x2), x3): Prefix token P S x1 x2 x3 Node number (preorder) 1 2 3 4 5 Meaning the whole ⨂ the ⨁ inside a b c A tensor power becomes, for example, (V⨁W)^2 → E2 S x1 x2.

Definition. To choose the next rewrite step, the oracle tnOracleStep walks the nodes in preorder (node 1, node 2, …). At the first node where any rule allowed by the goal applies, it applies the highest-priority such rule. The priority order for Expand is ZeroSum, ZeroProd, UnitProd, PowerExpand, DistRight, DistLeft, AssocSum, AssocProd. In effect, the oracle always works on the outermost, leftmost place that can change. That makes it fully predictable, which is what a net learning to imitate it needs. Example (goal Expand, on (a⨁b)⨂c): 1. Node 1 is P(S(a, b), c). DistRight applies: (A⨁B)⨂C → A⨂C ⨁ B⨂C. Result: a ⨂ c ⨁ b ⨂ c. 2. The new tree is S(P(a, c), P(b, c)). No Expand rule applies at any node, so the scan ends: this is the normal form. Longer example (goal Expand, on (V⊕W)^2): PowerExpand (node 1), DistRight (node 1), DistLeft (node 2), AssocSum (node 1), DistLeft (node 9). Result: V ⨂ V ⨁ V ⨂ W ⨁ W ⨂ V ⨁ W ⨂ W.

The three nets are built from the same parts. Token embedding. Each token is mapped to a learned vector of d numbers (d = 128 by default). The map is a lookup table: one row per vocabulary entry, adjusted during training. Position embedding. A second learned vector is added according to the token’s place in the sequence (1st, 2nd, …). Without it, the net could not tell P S x1 x2 x3 from the same tokens in another order. Self-attention17. Every position looks at every position, itself included. It computes how relevant each one is (scores, turned into weights that sum to 1), then takes the weighted mix of their vectors. Multi-head means this is done four times in parallel with different learned projections, so that different heads can follow different relations. For example, in ( x1 ⨁ x2 ) ⨂ x3, one head can learn to pair each ) with its (, while another links ⨂ with its operands. Feed-forward. A small two-layer network applied to each position separately (d → 4d → d, with a GELU non-linearity18). Residual connection19. Each part’s input is added to its output (output = x + f(x)). The block therefore only has to learn a correction, which keeps deep nets trainable. Layer normalisation20. After each residual addition, the d numbers at each position are rescaled to mean 0 and variance 1, then multiplied and shifted by learned amounts. This keeps the scale steady from block to block. Encoder. A stack of L blocks (L = 3 by default), each block being self-attention then feed-forward, both with residual connection and layer normalisation. It turns a sequence of tokens into a sequence of vectors, one per token, each informed by the whole sequence.

Token + position embeddings; encoder of L self-attention blocks; decoder of L blocks (causal self-attention, cross-attention to the encoder, feed-forward), each with residual connection and layer normalisation; softmax over the output vocabulary. Encoder: as in A.5, reading the lexer’s tokens. The input vocabulary has 32 entries: 13 operator and parenthesis spellings, the powers n1 … n9, the slots x1 … x8, and 0 and 1. Decoder: it writes the prefix form one token at a time. Each of its L blocks has three parts: Causal self-attention: like self-attention, but position i may look only at positions 1 … i, the tokens already written. It cannot see the future, which it will not have when it really generates. Cross-attention to the encoder21 — the decoder’s vectors ask questions of the encoder’s vectors. This is how the output is tied to the input string. Feed-forward: as in A.5. Softmax over the output vocabulary: at each step, the final vector is turned into a probability for each of the 22 output tokens (S, P, E2 … E9, x1 … x8, 0, 1, start <s> and end </s>). The most probable permitted token is written. Example (input ( x1 ⨁ x2 ) ⨂ x3). The decoder writes P, S, x1, x2, x3. The grammar constraint keeps a count of subtrees still owed: Written token none yet P S x1 x2 x3 Subtrees still owed 1 2 3 2 1 0 → stop An operator owes two subtrees and fills one (+1); an atom fills one (−1). A tree is complete exactly when the count reaches 0, so the output is always a well-formed tree.

h: A.7 Teacher forcing on random spellings
x: Teacher forcing on random trees written in random spellings (random glyphs, spacing and redundant parentheses), target = the tree’s prefix form. Random trees. The generator draws trees at random: depth 1 to 5, one to five atoms, with occasional 0, 𝟙 and powers ^2 and ^3. Random spellings. Each tree is written out as a string in a random way: - each operator gets a random glyph (⨁ ⊕ (+) +, or ⨂ ⊗ (x) *, in proportions 5 : 3 : 1 : 1); - spaces are random; - each subexpression is put in unnecessary parentheses with probability 8 %; - the atoms get random names, such as a, V', ψ_1 or B2. So one tree is seen in many disguises, and all of them have the same target. For P(S(x1, x2), x3), for example: (a⨁b)⨂c (ψ (+) V_1)*B' ((u⊕ w))⊗(H2) Target. The tree’s prefix form, framed by start and end: <s> P S x1 x2 x3 </s>. Teacher forcing22. During training, the decoder is not left to its own guesses. At every step it is shown the correct previous tokens, and is scored on predicting the next one: Decoder is given <s> <s> P <s> P S <s> P S x1 <s> P S x1 x2 <s> P S x1 x2 x3 Must predict P S x1 x2 x3 </s> The loss is the cross-entropy summed over all positions. All six predictions are trained at once (the causal mask of A.6 keeps each one honest), which makes training fast and stable. The weights are adjusted by NetTrain23 with its default optimiser, Adam24; the attention layers are Wolfram’s AttentionLayer25.

h: A.8 Two heads: which rule, at which node
x: The goal token is prepended to the prefix sequence; encoder as above; the rule head reads the goal position, the node head scores every position. Input. The goal is written as an extra first token. For Expand on (a⨁b)⨂c, the sequence is: Position 1 2 3 4 5 6 Token <Expand> P S x1 x2 x3 Tree node (the goal) 1 2 3 4 5 The encoder (A.5) turns this into six vectors. A head is a small output layer on top of them. Rule head (which rule): reads only the vector at position 1, the goal token. Through self-attention, that vector has gathered information about the whole expression. The head gives one probability per rule (11 rules), for example DistRight 0.92, AssocSum 0.03, and so on. Node head (at which node): gives every position a score (a pointer over the input, as in pointer networks26), and a softmax turns the scores into probabilities over the positions. Position k + 1 stands for tree node k: here position 2 (node 1, the outer ⨂) might get 0.95. Combining them with the legal-move mask. The exact engine lists the moves that are actually possible. Here there is only one: (DistRight, node 1). Each legal move is scored as p(rule) × p(node), and the best one is applied by the exact engine. The net therefore steers, but can never make an illegal or unsound step.

Transformer encoder, pooled regression. Definition. The encoder gives one vector per token. - Pooling combines them into a single vector for the whole expression; here, by taking their average. - Regression means the output is a real number, not a choice among classes. A small feed-forward head maps the pooled vector to three numbers, and training minimises the mean squared error against the exact values. - Besides the tokens, the net receives each atom’s log₂ dimension (0 for operators), added to the token’s vector. Example ((a⨁b)⨂c with dim a = 2, dim b = 3, dim c = 4).
